A function is invertible if and only if it's a one-to-one function. To determine which of the functions are one-to-one, we use the horizontal line test.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13932058/assets/95b1bd18e41cba7d6d1175f66be053ffea52a32fbb35e2ad1d126dbeb2d73baf.png)

From the above, we see that: 

- For graphs I and III, a horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line. Therefore, graphs I and III show one-to-one functions. This means that these functions are invertible.

- For graphs II and IV, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. So, these are not one-to-one functions. As a result, they are not invertible.

A function is invertible if and only if it's a one-to-one function. To determine which of the functions are one-to-one, we use the horizontal line test.

From the above, we see that:

  • For graphs I and III, a horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line. Therefore, graphs I and III show one-to-one functions. This means that these functions are invertible.
  • For graphs II and IV, some horizontal lines intersect the curve more than once. So, these are not one-to-one functions. As a result, they are not invertible.
